guardrail-gates.prompt: I want a short, interactive Khan Academy style lesson for non-engineers that explains why a file-permission gate that only checks how a path starts can be tricked, and what the safer gate designs do differently. Use the results from our notebook 10 (the data and key facts are in the input files). It should work well on a phone, and I'd like to be able to turn it into a GIF for LinkedIn later.
guardrail-gates.outcome: A step-by-step lesson (at least 4 steps) that shows how the prefix-only gate is fooled by .. steps, look-alike folder names and symbolic links, uses the real counts (5 of 14 forbidden requests allowed by the prefix gate, 0 of 14 by the resolving gates), lets the reader try at least one path themselves, and reads cleanly at phone width.

handoff-timelines.prompt: Make an animated visual that replays how the planner agent and its helper agents actually spent their time in our subagent handoff experiment (notebook 07; recorded runs are in the input files). A reader should see why the synchronous handoff took about 120 s while the async spawn finished in about 57 s, who was waiting for whom, and where the one late message got lost. Use the recorded timings, not made-up ones.
handoff-timelines.outcome: An animation driven by the recorded spans and events that shows agents' working and waiting time on a shared clock, makes the planner's blocked time in the synchronous handoff visible, states the real wall times (about 120 s and 57 s), shows the late message in level 3 arriving after it could be read, and can be paused or replayed.

invoice-checks.prompt: Build an interactive explainer for finance managers: when does it pay to let a cheap AI model handle invoice payments and only send the doubtful ones to the expensive model? Let them change the price of the expensive model and see which checking strategy is cheapest. Use the 72 test invoices from our econ notebook 21 (input files).
invoice-checks.outcome: An explorable where the reader moves the expensive model's price and sees the cost per invoice of each route update, with the break-even prices marked (about USD 0.0011 for the repeat check and USD 0.133 for Claude's check), the 14 of 72 invoices both checks accepted made concrete, and the assumptions about the cost of wrong payments labelled.

sql-safety-units.prompt: I need a visual for a LinkedIn post about notebook 05: 11 models each got 29 requests that would break the database rules. Most broke zero rules, but I want people to understand that zero out of 29 doesn't prove a model is safe. Make it engaging and honest about the uncertainty. Data is in the input files.
sql-safety-units.outcome: A visual that shows the 29 requests per model as countable items (Mistral Small 4 broke 7, Gemma 4 31B broke 3, the other 9 broke none), explains that 0 of 29 still allows a true rate up to about 12%, and makes the uncertainty tangible rather than only stating it.

forecast-guess.prompt: Make something engaging for our forecasting notebook (16): readers should get a feel for how hard it is to beat 'just repeat last week' when forecasting Ontario electricity demand, and how much the pretrained forecasting models actually improve on it. The example forecast and the scores are in the input files.
forecast-guess.outcome: An engaging explainer built on the real example origin (14 days of history, the actual week, seasonal naive and the models' forecasts) that conveys how close repeating last week comes, reports the headline relative error (about 0.86 for the best pretrained models versus 1.0 for repeating last week), and does not overstate the improvement from one example week.
